articles.title: Yahoo Sports and Apple TV team up to deliver live MLB and MLS alternate broadcasts
articles.summary: The altcasts will stream across Yahoo Sports platforms and feature Yahoo Sports experts on the call.
articles.body:
Between games, fans turn to Yahoo Sports shows Baseball Bar-B-Cast and The Cooligans for analysis from baseball analysts Jake Mintz and Jordan Shusterman and soccer analysts Alexis Guerreros and Christian Polanco . Now, those familiar voices can be heard during live broadcasts, bringing an added layer of analysis and perspective to the game as it unfolds.

Yahoo Sports and Apple TV 1 are teaming up to deliver alternate broadcasts of live "Friday Night Baseball" and Major League Soccer games. With Yahoo Sports experts on the call, these altcasts will stream across the Yahoo Sports website and app and feature unique camera angles provided by Apple TV.

"We're thrilled to pair our expert voices with Apple TV's live coverage to give fans on Yahoo a fun new way to watch 'Friday Night Baseball' and MLS action," said Jarrod Schwarz, General Manager, Yahoo Sports. "These broadcasts will feature the insight, personality, and chemistry that make Baseball Bar-B-Cast and The Cooligans so popular, and we can't wait to see that energy show up during some of the season's biggest games."

"Friday Night Baseball" on Apple TV live on Yahoo

Baseball Bar-B-Cast hosts Jake Mintz and Jordan Shusterman will broadcast the first two innings of a pair of games from the "Friday Night Baseball" on Apple TV package, both of which have playoff implications:

Friday, Sept. 4: Detroit Tigers at Cleveland Guardians

Friday, Sept. 18: Philadelphia Phillies at New York Mets

The Yahoo Sports senior MLB writers will also host pre-game shows for each contest. All video for the Yahoo Sports streams will originate from the main Apple TV broadcast feed. Following the conclusion of the two-inning altcast, Apple TV subscribers can continue watching the full game on Apple TV.

The Cooligans duo of Alexis Guerreros and Christian Polanco will be on the call for a pair of significant MLS tilts:

Wednesday, Sept. 16: 2026 Michelob ULTRA Campeones Cup, featuring reigning MLS Cup champion Inter Miami CF pitted against defending Liga MX champion Cruz Azul

Wednesday, Oct. 28: Inter Miami CF vs FC Cincinnati

Each MLS altcast will include pregame coverage and the full match. The altcast will showcase a range of camera angles provided by Apple TV and MLS Productions, from the main broadcast feed to distinctive perspectives—including a referee cam and dedicated feed shot entirely on iPhone.

The Yahoo Sports altcasts will also serve to help educate fans on how to watch Apple TV's "Friday Night Baseball" and MLS broadcasts. Each stream will feature a direct link to the Apple TV app, where fans can subscribe to watch the main broadcast of the featured altcast matchups along with the platform's full slate of games. In addition, Yahoo Sports will promote Apple TV's exclusive "Friday Night Baseball" broadcasts and global coverage of MLS through on-site advertising, email marketing, social promotion, "how to watch" articles, Daily Draw games and more.

1 To watch "Friday Night Baseball" and MLS on Apple TV, viewers are required to have an Apple TV subscription. An Apple TV subscription does not include third-party branded subscription services, or content available for rental or purchase in the Apple TV app.

articles.title: Yahoo Sports, Apple TV team up for ‘Baseball Bar-B-Cast’ and ‘The Cooligans’ altcasts
articles.summary: Yahoo Sports and Apple TV are partnering for a series of altcasts starring the hosts of the Baseball Bar-B-Cast and The Cooligans. The two companies announce...
articles.body:
Yahoo Sports and Apple TV are partnering for a series of altcasts starring the hosts of the Baseball Bar-B-Cast and The Cooligans .

The two companies announced on Wednesday that Apple TV's MLB and MLS packages will feature a series of altcasts before those respective seasons end. Jake Mintz and Jordan Shusterman, co-hosts of Yahoo's Baseball Bar-B-Cast , will call the first two innings of Apple TV's broadcasts of the Detroit Tigers-Cleveland Guardians game on Sept. 4, and the Philadelphia Phillies-New York Mets game on Sept. 18. Mintz and Shusterman will also host pregame shows for each broadcast. The first two innings of each game will stream across Yahoo Sports' platforms before transitioning to Apple TV for the last seven innings.

Additionally, Yahoo and Apple will team up for a pair of MLS altcasts featuring the co-hosts of The Cooligans , stand-up comedians Alexis Guerreros and Christian Polanco. The duo will call two games: the Campeones Cup between reigning MLS Cup champion Inter Miami and defending Liga MX champion Cruz Azul on Sept. 16, and a game between Inter Miami and FC Cincinnati on Oct. 28. Both matches will stream in full on Yahoo Sports platforms. The altcast will feature "a range of camera angles provided by Apple TV," including a referee cam and a feed shot entirely on iPhone.

While these altcasts are pretty limited in scope, they should offer some decent cross-promotion between both Yahoo and Apple's sports offerings. At the very least, they'll give fans some additional options when tuning in for a handful of the more important regular-season games Apple TV will broadcast for either league this year.

articles.title: MLB Player Drops Bold Statement on Potential Work Stoppage for 2027 Season Amid Salary Cap Talks
articles.summary: As the MLB playoffs draw nearer, many around the majors are already looking ahead to the expected labor battle this offseason.
articles.body:
As the MLB playoffs draw nearer, many around the majors are already looking ahead to the expected labor battle this offseason.

ESPN spoke to multiple MLB players who continued to push back against the idea of implementing a salary cap in the next collective bargaining agreement. One player had a bold declaration about the potential work stoppage for the 2027 season.

"Get ready to see a bunch of schoolteachers and whatnot out there, because we're not playing if there's a cap," an NL infielder on a lucrative contract said.

Despite the players making their stance clear, team owners have maintained their desire for a salary cap system that would help improve the league's competitive balance. Players were asked if they expect there to be "a lengthy lockout" that impacts next season, and many answered affirmatively.

"Yes. That's easy," one NL free-agent-to-be coming off multiyear deal said. "Nothing gets done until a deadline. We managed to avoid it last time. Hoping for the same."

"I would lean towards yes," an NL reliever on two-year contract added. "I think it ends up, if i'm guessing, I would say it ends up probably about how 2021 ended up."

Still, other players continued to hold out hope that there won't be any missed games in 2027, as there's still a lot of time for the two sides to reach an agreement.

"If it's a yes or no answer, I'm going to go with hopefully not. I don't think so. I hope both sides figure it out. It makes no sense for there to be a lockout," an AL infielder making eight figures this season said. "And the owners saying it as far out as they have, yes, there's going to be a lockout, yes, there's going to be a lockout. And I just hope it doesn't affect [the season] and we figure it out before then."

"We're not missing games. I'm holding onto that hope," a reliever with union leadership role said. "We're gonna put that out there and see what happens."

The MLBPA has remained steadfast in its opposition of MLB's latest proposals.

In a statement issued on Aug. 27, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer said owners' efforts to "establish an artificial free agency window, subject to a salary cap, would reduce player leverage and create a game of musical chairs pitting player vs. player."

articles.title: Stan Kroenke Reportedly Plans to Build New $2.5B Angels Stadium After Buying MLB Team
articles.summary: Stan Kroenke reportedly isn't going to wait long to make significant changes surrounding the Los Angeles Angels after purchasing the team.
articles.body:
Stan Kroenke reportedly isn't going to wait long to make significant changes surrounding the Los Angeles Angels after purchasing the team.

Barry M. Bloom of Forbes reported Arte Moreno tentatively sold the American League West team to Kroenke on Tuesday at a valuation of $4.5 billion. The expectation is the sale will be finalized early in 2027 after being approved by MLB.

Bloom also reported Kroenke plans on building a new $2.5 billion stadium to replace Angel Stadium.

Angel Stadium opened in 1966 and has been refurbished multiple times.

Building a new stadium will be nothing new for Kroenke, who oversaw the construction of SoFi Stadium and the complex surrounding it for $5.5 billion as the owner of the NFL's Los Angeles Rams.

Kroenke is also familiar with success as a franchise owner, as the Rams, NHL's Colorado Avalanche, NBA's Denver Nuggets and MLS' Colorado Rapids have all won league titles during his tenure. What's more, Arsenal won the most recent Premier League title.

"Look at his track record," Angels star Mike Trout said. "It's all there. So, I'm super excited to meet him, get to know him a little bit, and see where it goes."

Angels fans are certainly hoping the ownership change leads to more success on the field.

Los Angeles has made the playoffs just once since 2009 and saw that postseason appearance come to a swift end with a sweep in the 2014 American League Division Series.

Trout is an all-time great, but the team struggled to find success even when he was teammates with Shohei Ohtani.

Bloom noted Kroenke is worth $24.3 billion, which will make him the richest owner in MLB with the New York Mets' Steve Cohen at $23 billion. Quickly putting billions into a new stadium would suggest the new Angels owner will be willing to spend to find some of that success that has been missing for so long.

articles.title: Stan Kroenke's record-setting LA Angels purchase should make longterm MLB lockout less likely
articles.summary: Stan Kroenke's record $4 billion purchase of the Los Angeles Angels undermines Major League Baseball owners' claims about struggling businesses.
articles.body: If there were any remaining doubts as to the viability and earning potential of Major League Baseball teams, this week's news should end it. Out of seemingly nowhere, Stan Kroenke, one of the wealthiest people in America, agreed to purchase a majority stake in the Los Angeles Angels from longtime owner Arte Moreno. It had been rumored in recent years that Moreno was considering a sale, but a deal never materialized. Until now. The price Kroenke paid for the Angels was estimated at a record-breaking $4 billion, representing an enormous return for Moreno who purchased the franchise for just over $180 million from the Walt Disney Company back in 2003. It was also, at first glance, a significant price for an organization that has the longest postseason drought in baseball. Despite having Mike Trout and Shohei Ohtani on the same roster for several seasons, the Angels have not reached the playoffs since 2014. ARTE MORENO ERA OFFICIALLY OVER AS ANGELS SELL TO RAMS OWNER STAN KROENKE FOR $4B The immediate question, then, is why? Why would Kroenke, an eminently talented and successful businessman who's already principal owner of organizations like the Los Angeles Rams, Arsenal FC and the Denver Nuggets, now turn his attention to, well, the polar opposite? And the answer explains why so much of the information coming from Major League Baseball and the league's owners is misleading, at best. With the Collective Bargaining Agreement between the league and MLB Players Association expiring at the end of the season, it's widely expected that the owners will lock the players out until a new deal can be reached. The largest point of contention between the two sides is disagreement over a potential salary cap. Players have, for decades, said a salary cap is a red line they will never accept. While owners are hoping to take advantage of widespread, and inaccurate, fan sentiment believing that a salary cap is necessary for the league to achieve competitive balance. Another key aspect of their argument is that the business of baseball is not as strong as it should be. That franchise valuations have lagged behind the NFL because that league has a salary cap, ensuring relatively fixed costs for players. As well as that the collapse of the local sports television networks have negatively impacted their bottom lines. Here's the problem with that, though: there have been two MLB organizations to sell in 2026: the San Diego Padres and now the Angels. Both set records for the largest ever purchase price of an MLB team, and neither organization has a local broadcast partner, like say, the Dodgers do with Spectrum SportsNet LA or the Yankees do with YES. If the loss in revenue from those television deals was so catastrophic, why are these two organizations worth so much money? MLBPA Interim Executive Director Bruce Meyer told OutKick that it shows the "overall health" of the industry is outstanding and that owners are realizing "huge profits." "Arte Moreno bought the Angels in 2003 for $183.5 million. His ownership failures are well documented, from highlighting that winning wasn’t a priority, to unsubstantiated complaints about profitability. Yet despite his long record of underachievement, Moreno sold the team to Stan Kroenke for a record $4-$4.5 billion, netting a multi-billion dollar return on his purchase. It's a perfect example of the overall health of the industry, and the huge profits owners realize from owning baseball teams—value which is generated by the talents of players." Kroenke's not one to make bad investments, nor one to rush to judgment on a $4 billion purchase. So why'd he do it? Because, as Meyer says, baseball is booming. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! The Angels are a potential gold mine waiting to be taken advantage of by competent ownership. Even without a competitive team, for more than a decade, the Angels still rank 13th in baseball in average attendance with nearly 33,000 tickets sold per game. Already, reports have suggested Kroenke intends to build a brand new, multi-billion dollar stadium to take advantage of a fanbase ready and willing to support a winning team. Trout, the long-suffering franchise icon, said as much. "I'm excited," he said Tuesday after the news broke. "Look, the track record — it's there." "Seeing the reaction from the fans and some of the guys and the whole vibe, I think it was needed for a fresh start," he continued. "The biggest thing is getting that feeling of getting that winning culture back and having that vibe in the clubhouse." This is a sleeping giant in the nation's second-largest media market. The Padres down the road sell out most of their games. A more appropriately-run Angels team could be next. Then there's the real estate investment component. Angel Stadium sits on a massive, underdeveloped parking lot. Kroenke is almost certainly looking to tear up that wasted concrete and build mixed-use development nearby. Shops, restaurants, townhomes, apartments, condos, you name it. Build a ballpark village next to a brand new facility, and people will come. This model has already been demonstrated by The Battery, a Braves-owned development next to Truist Park in the Atlanta area. New York Mets owner Steve Cohen intends to build a casino on underutilized land next to Citi Field. Billionaire owners are capitalizing on their baseball franchises to create real estate portfolios that rely on fans from those teams. PADRES STRIKE DEAL TO SELL TO INVESTOR GROUP LED BY PRIVATE EQUITY BILLIONAIRE, VOWS WORLD SERIES CHAMPIONSHIP That's well within their rights, of course, and it's smart business. It also can create a better experience for fans, who can come to the ballpark earlier or stay afterward with friends and family. The problem from the players' perspective is that when the league says they want to base a salary cap on the revenue they bring in, they exclude this ancillary, connected, income from the calculation. Kroenke bought the Angels for a gigantic price because he doesn't care whether a salary cap happens or not. None of the owners care about a salary cap, at least as it pertains to competitive balance. They want to limit spending on players and retain more profits. That's it. OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD They claim their businesses are struggling. That they're losing money and don't turn enough yearly profit. But their exploding franchise values keep undermining those claims and proving that the opposite is true. Even the 53-86 Angels, on pace for their first ever 100 loss season, are worth a fortune. That's the truth, regardless of what they say to win fan support.

articles.title: Was Ronald Acuña Jr.'s latest home run a sign that the Braves' slugger is back?
articles.summary: The 200th long ball of Acuña's career comes amid a season in which the 2023 NL MVP has looked far from his best self.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON — For just the second time this season, Ronald Acuña Jr. sent a high heater screaming into the seats.

On a wet, sparsely attended Wednesday in the nation's capital, Atlanta's sweet-swinging showman absolutely unloaded on a 0-0 fastball from Nationals reliever Max Kranick. Acuña, bat still in hand, strolled toward first base while admiring his handiwork. Six seconds later, when the baseball crested over the left-field wall, Acuña pointed toward the sky in celebration and, perhaps, relief. He hadn't homered in nearly three weeks. And this was the 200th long ball of his career, making Acuña the single fastest player in MLB history to reach 200 homers and 200 steals.

"It's an honor to [be atop that list]," Acuña said postgame. "I know how hard I've worked to be here."

Acuña has lived quite the baseball life, enduring more before his 30th birthday than most do in a career. Yes, he was blessed by the heavens with a rocket right arm and lightning-quick bat. But the hardball gods also gave him two torn ACLs, one on each knee, taking away time he'll never get back. He watched the 2021 Braves make history from the dugout.

That tumultuous journey makes milestones such as the one Acuña reached Wednesday all the more gratifying. But in the context of this Braves season and this Acuña season, it was particularly encouraging to see the scuffling slugger demolish a high heater, something he has struggled to do all year.

"When he's getting to heaters," Braves skipper Walt Weiss said following his team's 9-0 drubbing of Washington , "that's a good sign."

The Braves will hope it's also a sign of things to come, considering what an odd, disjointed season it has been for their 28-year-old star.

A nagging left hamstring has twice pushed Acuña onto the shelf, forcing him to miss more than 50 games. And even during the windows of health, he has looked far from his best self. The 2023 NL MVP is sporting career-low figures in batting average and on-base percentage. Among the 204 hitters with at least 350 plate appearances this season, Acuña's .404 slugging percentage ranks 119th. He has been worth just 0.9 fWAR, the 11th-best mark on his own team.

And things haven't been going any better since he returned from his most recent IL stint on July 27; since then, Acuña is rocking an uncharacteristically underwhelming .217/.289/.380 line.

After a shocking, October-less 2025, the Braves have put themselves in phenomenal position to return to the postseason. With their victory and the Phillies' loss Wednesday , the Braves retain a four-game lead in the NL East with an 83-57 record. That resurgence is most attributable to huge offensive campaigns from Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II, as well as a Cy Young-caliber showing from the eternally brilliant Chris Sale . The bullpen has also been dynamite, and Weiss should win Manager of the Year.

But while Acuña, in spurts, has certainly helped the cause, the 2026 version of him has produced more like a supporting character than a franchise cornerstone.

Really, it has all been about the fastball.

For years, Acuña was one of the league's most dangerous hitters against heaters. That was particularly true during his historic 2023 campaign, but even as recently as last season, the twitchy outfielder ranked ninth in Statcast's run-value metric against four-seamers. Entering play Wednesday, he ranked 342nd this season.

His struggles against fastballs have been particularly loud at the top of the strike zone and just above it. Here's a chart via TruMedia showing Acuña's expected slugging percentage on fastballs in the upper-third and higher since 2021.

And here's that same trend visualized with heat maps:

This year, Acuña is also chasing fastballs up far more often than he did in any other season in his career. Last season, his chase rate on high heaters was 7.3%. This year, it's 21.4% (which, to be clear, is still below league-average). Teams and pitchers have certainly noticed; Acuña, since returning from the IL, has seen the sixth-highest percentage of four-seam fastballs of any qualified hitter.

Given his age and injury history — again, Acuña has had both of his ACLs surgically repaired — this all qualifies as a concerning trend. Because even though his raw bat speed remains near-elite, it has declined by a full mile per hour since 2023. Athleticism is a full-body endeavor. Those margins matter. Pitchers are throwing harder than ever. A millisecond can be the difference between dominance and despair.

It's on Acuña, then, to make the necessary adjustments. And there are multiple avenues. He could cut his chase rate, set his sights lower and force pitchers into the zone more often. He could cheat to heaters against certain pitchers in certain spots. He could do offseason bat-speed training. He could seek to shorten his swing path.

Acuña admitted after Wednesday's game that he hasn't made any major adjustments in regard to elevated fastballs. Instead, he's sticking with his routine, likely in the hope that the further he gets from his injuries, the quicker, the better he'll feel in the box. His manager expressed a similar sentiment.

"Ronald, he's capable of pretty much anything on the field, you know?" Weiss said. "And he's missed a lot of time in the last couple years. It takes time for those guys to get caught back up to the speed of the game."

Was Wednesday's blast a harbinger? Is Acuña starting to shake off the rust? Or was it merely an aberration, and adjustments are still necessary?

Time, of course, will tell. But this season's clock is ticking, ticking as October beckons for Acuña and the Braves.

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani Shutdown as Pitcher Being Considered amid Injury, Dodgers' Dave Roberts Says
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani may not pitch again the rest of the season
articles.body:
Shohei Ohtani may not pitch again the rest of the season

Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters Wednesday the team is considering shutting down Ohtani as a pitcher for the rest of 2026 but has not fully made that decision.

He also said playing corner outfield is "not on the table."

Report: New Angels Owner Wants $2.5B Stadium

At this point, the 2026 Dodgers are accustomed to playing without Ohtani as a pitcher.

He last appeared on the mound on July 3 but has continued to be one of the league's best hitters with a .281/.383/.530 slash line, 30 home runs and 80 RBI. While he is at his most valuable when he is thriving both at the plate and on the mound, Ohtani has remained one of the best players in all of baseball as just a hitter.

Los Angeles also has no shortage of star power in its starting rotation.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow make up arguably the best starting rotation in baseball and will be a daunting matchup for any opponent come playoff time. A third straight World Series title could be in the cards simply based on the starting pitching alone.

While losing a pitcher of Ohtani's quality from the rotation may be impossible to overcome for most teams, the Dodgers are well equipped to continue thriving.

What this may have the biggest impact on is the National League MVP race. Chicago Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong is a massive -1,500 favorite (bet $1,500 to win $100) on FanDuel Sportsbook with Ohtani a distant second at +750.

Ohtani's pitching is what makes him so unique, especially in MVP discussions. But if he spends the majority of the season as a designated hitter while Crow-Armstrong is playing elite defense in centerfield and putting up similar or better offensive numbers, the Cubs star may continue to pull away in the discussion.

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani injury: Dodgers manager Dave Roberts says shutting down star as a pitcher for the season is 'an option'
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani might have already thrown his last pitch of 2026.
articles.body:
It's no longer a given that Shohei Ohtani will pitch again in 2026.

The Los Angeles Dodgers' superstar has been working purely as a designated hitter since July 3 due to a left knee issue that required a lubricant injection during the All-Star break . The team hoped he could return as a pitcher in an abbreviated fashion Sunday, but a bullpen session days earlier didn't go well enough to put Ohtani on the mound .

When asked if there is a deadline to make such a decision, Roberts indicated that the team is in no rush:

"There's no hard timeline because any inning that he gives us is additive, given his roster availability. To say that you could give us one inning or two innings is not valuable, that's not true. The cost is does it affect his health? There's really no timeline, definitive deadline to say, 'Hey, this is when we're going to stop.'"

Like last year, Ohtani's return as a pitcher is complicated by his value to the Dodgers as a hitter. The plan was never for him to go on a rehab assignment, and Roberts indicated that the team has been monitoring whether Ohtani's pitching rehab interferes with his offensive performance:

"I certainly know the value of him pitching. But if you're not 100 percent, there's possibly some bleed-in to the performance offensively. That's just kind of me theorizing. It's his decision, honestly, if he feels like he's capable and then we'll run the play out until it doesn't make any sense."

Ohtani has slashed .269/.344/.538 since his last start as a pitcher, still productive but off the MVP-level pace he has set so far in his Dodgers career.

Roberts' comments came a day after Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said he believes Ohtani will pitch again, via The Athletic's Katie Woo . Friedman did not commit to a timeline, either.

One thing the Dodgers won't be doing is trying Ohtani out as a corner outfielder, a position he played in Japan and in a few late-inning situations for the Los Angeles Angels in 2021. When asked about that idea, Roberts said it was "off the table."

The good news for the Dodgers is they don't need Ohtani pitching to have a formidable postseason rotation. The quartet of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow looms as one of the best units in baseball, assuming everyone stays healthy (never a given).

The Dodgers also have a World Series under their belt with Ohtani as a DH only, having triumphed in 2024 despite far larger rotation concerns than they have right now.

The situation also has award implications, as Chicago Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong has made an excellent case to win NL MVP with Ohtani delivering value on offense only over the past two months. Of course, there's still nearly all of September to go.

articles.title: What really happened between Bryce Harper and Kayla Harper as their young love grew into something much bigger? The love story behind the MLB star’s private world
articles.summary: MLB News: Bryce Harper has spent most of his life in the baseball spotlight. Away from the Phillies star’s biggest moments, however, there has been another stor.
articles.body: Bryce Harper has spent most of his life in the baseball spotlight. Away from the Phillies star’s biggest moments, however, there has been another story quietly unfolding. His relationship with Kayla Harper began when they were teenagers and grew alongside a career that made Bryce one of baseball’s most recognizable names. Years later, Kayla offered a rare glimpse into what that life has been like and why some parts of it can still hit close to home.Kayla Harper reveals why watching Bryce Harper get judged has become the hardest part of their life in the spotlightLong before Bryce Harper became an established MLB star, he and Kayla were already part of each other’s lives.The two met as teenagers and eventually built a relationship that continued as Bryce’s baseball career moved from promise to the major leagues. Kayla has known him from a time when he was simply a young baseball player rather than a household name.Their relationship also grew as the attention around Bryce became harder to escape.Harper entered the professional baseball world with enormous expectations. Success brought even more attention, while difficult stretches naturally brought criticism. For Kayla, watching that happen from such a close distance created a perspective that fans and commentators could never really have.She has seen the person behind the player.The couple eventually married and built a family together. They now share four children, giving them a life that exists well beyond the baseball field.That private side became especially important during their joint appearance on Kristin Cavallari’s “Let’s Be Honest” podcast.Kayla generally keeps away from the spotlight, which made her openness during the conversation stand out. Instead of focusing on Bryce’s statistics or achievements, she spoke about what it feels like to watch someone she loves become the subject of constant public opinion.When Cavallari asked what she considered the hardest part of being married to a professional athlete, Kayla did not point to the long seasons or the pressure of playing at the highest level.She pointed to the way people judge Bryce.Kayla explained that criticism of his performance was not what affected her most. What hurt was hearing people question his character and describe him in ways that did not match the person she knew at home.That became an emotional moment for Kayla as she struggled to hold back tears.Bryce Harper learned to tune out the noise while Kayla struggled to watch from the sidelinesKayla also admitted that staying quiet has not always been easy.Earlier in their relationship, she sometimes responded when people criticized Bryce. She described herself as someone who can be outspoken and sarcastic, especially when she feels someone is being unfair.With time, however, she learned that answering every negative comment rarely accomplished anything.Bryce appears to have developed an even tougher skin.Having dealt with public attention since he was very young, the Phillies star said he does not care much about the opinions of strangers. His reasoning is simple. The people criticizing him are not the ones sitting around his Thanksgiving table or walking through his front door.That difference says a lot about their relationship.Kayla sees the criticism through the eyes of someone who loves Bryce and knows him away from baseball. Bryce has spent years learning to separate his public image from his private life.Their story is therefore about more than an MLB player and his wife. It is about two people who grew up together while one of them became famous and the other watched that fame change how strangers saw the person she loved.After 16 years of marriage, Kayla and Bryce have built a family and a life that exists far beyond the noise surrounding baseball. They share four children, Krew Aron, Brooklyn Elizabeth, Kamryn Ray and Hayes Three.Their recent conversation offered a rare look at the people behind the public image.For Bryce, criticism is part of the career he chose as a young athlete. For Kayla, it can feel much more personal because she remembers the person he was before the fame.And that may be the most revealing part of their story. Behind the MLB star is a husband and father she has known since their teenage years. Behind the wife who became emotional is someone who has spent years watching the world form opinions about a person she knows in a completely different way.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rams legend Eric Dickerson speaks on Los Angeles Angels sale, says new owner Stan Kroenke 'likes winning'
articles.summary: Eric Dickerson praised Stan Kroenke as a winner while throwing the first pitch at Angel Stadium amid the Angels' $4 billion ownership change.
articles.body: Rams legend Eric Dickerson took the mound at Angel Stadium on Wednesday night to throw out the ceremonial first pitch before the Angels faced the Yankees in Anaheim. Celebration continues across Southern California after longtime Angels owner Arte Moreno agreed to sell the team Tuesday. The fans are getting a new leader in Stan Kroenke, a proven winner who also owns the Rams. Speaking with MLB.com’s Rhett Bollinger before taking the field, Dickerson offered a glowing review of Kroenke. "Kind of quiet but a really good businessman as you can tell. But Stan likes winning. I can tell you that right now. He likes winning," Dickerson said. Dickerson, who serves as an ambassador for the Rams, also joked about the timing of his visit to Anaheim. WORLD CUP HERO THROWS OUT FIRST PITCH AT YANKEE STADIUM AND SETS THE BAR HIGH FOR ALL OTHER ATHLETES "When I saw it, I was like, ‘I’m supposed to throw the first pitch out,’" he said. Kroenke Sports & Entertainment agreed Tuesday to purchase a controlling interest in the Angels at a reported $4 billion valuation. The transaction is expected to close in early 2027, pending approval from Major League Baseball. HERE'S WHAT THE SAN DIEGO PADRES RECORD $3.9 BILLION SALE MEANS FOR MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL The deal would end Moreno’s 23-year run as the Angels’ controlling owner. Moreno purchased the team from Disney for $184 million in 2003, after the Angels won their first World Series. The Angels enjoyed early success under Moreno, but the franchise has struggled for more than a decade. The team has endured 11 consecutive losing seasons, has not reached the postseason since 2014 and has not won a playoff game since 2009. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kroenke inherits one of baseball’s most long-suffering fan bases, but his winning track record speaks for itself. His sports empire features a Super Bowl with the Rams, an NBA title with the Nuggets, a Stanley Cup with the Avalanche and a Premier League title with Arsenal. With a proven winner taking charge, Angels fans finally have reason to believe change is coming. On Tuesday night, years of "sell the team" chants gave way to a new refrain: "Goodbye, Arte." articles.title: 10 Strong Opinions on the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline, 1 Month Later
articles.summary: One month has passed since the dust settled on the 2026 MLB trade deadline, and that's a big enough sample size in the sports world for some strong opinions.
articles.body:
One month has passed since the dust settled on the 2026 MLB trade deadline, and that's a big enough sample size in the sports world for some strong opinions.

The New York Yankees move to land Luis García Jr. has looked like a stroke of genius given his early production and importance to the lineup, while other high-profile moves have not played out quite so well.

Meanwhile, the Toronto Blue Jays actually got better after selling, while the Chicago Cubs bullpen somehow got worse after a marquee addition.

Let's dive into our 10 strongest opinions about the 2026 deadline, one month after the league's annual flurry of trade activity.

The Rockies Were Right to Keep Jake McCarthy

Hunter Goodman, Jake McCarthy and Mickey Moniak looked like the Rockies' most valuable trade chips heading into deadline day, but all three ended up staying put as they opted instead for a few smaller-scale moves.

After hitting .204 with a 63 OPS+ for the D-backs in 2025, McCarthy looked like the most obvious sell-high candidate of the bunch, and it seemed like the Rockies might have missed their chance to flip him for a quality return.

Following an August where he batted .288/.328/.441 with 10 extra-base hits and nine steals, McCarthy now sports the following season line:

109 OPS+, .290/.331/.475, 49 XBH (14 HR), 72 RBI, 26 SB

With two years of club control remaining, a strong finish could make him a more valuable trade chip this offseason than he was at the deadline, with a longer runway of production under his belt.

The starting rotation was understandably the focal point for the Cubs at the deadline, and they did well to bolster the staff with the additions of Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.

The relief corps seemingly took a backseat, but it was not ignored by any means, as former top prospect Moisés Ballesteros was part of a package used to acquire Angels strikeout artist Ryan Zeferjahn, who has club control through 2030.

The thinking seemed to be that Zeferjahn was a potentially impactful enough addition that he could slot into a high-leverage role and stabilize the bullpen as a result.

Instead, he has struggled to a 7.20 ERA while allowing runs in five of his 11 appearances, and the entire relief corps now looks like a ticking time bomb heading into October. There is still time for the pieces to fall into place, but right now the bullpen looks worse than it did on Aug. 2.

The Entire League Was Sleeping on Jeff McNeil

It was difficult to find an obvious trade candidate on the Athletics roster this summer, but Jeff McNeil offered some buy-low potential as a seasoned veteran with defensive versatility.

He was batting .251/.309/.332 heading into deadline day, which, coupled with the roughly $3.3 million remaining on his salary, led to virtually no trade buzz as he ended up staying put.

Since the trade deadline, McNeil is batting .318/.344/.489 with six doubles, three home runs and 15 RBI in 94 plate appearances, and suddenly that $3.3 million price tag doesn't look so bad.

As a potential bench bat or part-time player for the stretch run, he would have been a useful pickup for almost any contender.

Jazz Chisholm responds to Red Sox broadcaster's comments

Casey Mize's Breakout Might Have Been a Product of Comerica Park

The Padres pulled off a buzzer-beater on deadline day to bolster a starting rotation in serious need of help, acquiring Casey Mize from the Tigers.

The former No. 1 overall pick was enjoying the best season of his career at the time with a 2.70 ERA and 2.57 FIP in 86.2 innings.

The price they paid was steep for the two-month rental, with Top 100 prospect Kash Mayfield in the package that went the other way.

Not only has the deal not worked out for San Diego, as Mize has a 6.26 ERA over his first five starts, but we're quickly drifting into "costing himself money in free agency" territory.

Considering his stellar 2.36 ERA over 45.2 innings at Comerica Park before the trade, it might be time to start asking whether Mize had simply become really good at pitching in the only home ballpark he had ever known. A case for the Tigers to re-sign him this winter?

The Blue Jays Perfectly Threaded the Buy/Sell Needle

The Blue Jays were 52-60 on Aug. 2, which put them ninth in the AL wild-card standings, but only 4.5 games out of a playoff spot due to the ugly nature of the No. 3 wild-card candidate pool.

Rather than fully waving the white flag, they did some short-term selling by moving impending free agents Kevin Gausman and Daulton Varsho while also landing controllable major league pieces José Soriano and Spencer Arrighetti to replenish the rotation.

After going 17-11 in August, the Blue Jays are still right in the thick of the playoff race at just 2.5 games behind the Guardians for the No. 3 wild-card spot.

Soriano (5 GS, 4.13 ERA, 28.1 IP) has slotted nicely into Gausman's spot in the rotation, while Brett Bateman (92 PA, .317/.367/.390) has taken over as the everyday center fielder and leadoff hitter after he was acquired from the Cubs in the Gausman deal.

The decision to thread the needle between buying and selling might just end in an improved 2027 outlook and a trip to the 2026 postseason.

I Was Wrong About Tyler Mahle to the Braves

Here was my deadline day assessment of the Braves move to acquire Tyler Mahle, who had a 5.13 ERA in 94.2 innings with the Giants at the time of the deal:

"Is Tyler Mahle going to start a playoff game? If the answer is no, the Braves didn't do enough at the trade deadline. If the answer is yes, the Braves didn't do enough at the trade deadline. Outfielder Lane Thomas and reliever Brent Suter are solid complementary pickups, but this team needed a No. 2 starter to shoulder the load alongside Chris Sale."

With a 1.48 ERA in 30.1 innings and four quality starts in five outings, Mahle has in fact been exactly what the Braves needed as a co-anchor to the rotation behind ace Chris Sale.

His 2.86 FIP doesn't scream significant regression waiting around the corner either, and at this point it would be surprising if he's not on the mound to start a playoff game in October.

I Was Also Wrong About Taylor Ward to the Mariners

Here was my quick-hit reaction on the Mariners move to land Taylor Ward, who had a .383 on-base percentage and 111 OPS+ in 111 games with the Orioles:

"For a Mariners team that ranks 26th in the majors with a .310 on-base percentage, he should upgrade a major weakness while plugging a hole at one of the outfield corners."

I gave the Mariners side of the trade an "A" grade.

Through 75 plate appearances in a Mariners uniform, Ward is hitting a robust .121/.227/.152 with one extra-base hit and a 29.3 percent strikeout rate.

The Mariners had the lowest-scoring offense in baseball in August (95 runs, 3.52 runs per game), and their .304 on-base percentage was actually a step backward with Ward in the fold.

Liam Hicks Was the Steal of the 2026 Trade Deadline

The Rays have been searching for stability at the catcher position since their inception as a franchise in 1998, and they had used the light-hitting tandem of Nick Fortes and Hunter Feduccia for most of the season prior to the deadline.

Rarely a team willing to part with top prospect capital, they sent a package of three players ranked outside their organization's top 10 list to the Marlins in exchange for Liam Hicks.

Just a year removed from being a Rule 5 pick, Hicks had a 127 OPS+ with 14 home runs and 62 RBI at the time of the trade, though middling batted-ball metrics and his lack of track record rarely put him in the top-tier catcher conversation.

Since the trade, he has continued to rake, hitting .328/.425/.522 for a 163 OPS+, and he has settled in as the team's primary cleanup hitter. With club control through the 2030 season, it's quickly shaping up to be the biggest steal of the deadline and a top-tier deadline deal in Tampa Bay history.

Erik Miller, Not Adley Rutschman, Is the Red Sox Game-Changing Addition

No trade deadline deal was a bigger shock than the Orioles sending former No. 1 overall pick and franchise cornerstone Adley Rutschman to the division-rival Red Sox in exchange for a massive haul of prospect talent.

It dwarfed the rest of Boston's deadline activity, but the team did also make the surprising decision to cut ties with longtime top prospect Marcelo Mayer, flipping him to the Giants for a lefty reliever.

That lefty reliever, named Erik Miller, has since emerged as the best setup arm in the Red Sox bullpen. The 28-year-old has a minuscule 0.79 ERA and a 20-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 11.1 innings, with two holds and a win.

Meanwhile, Rutschman is 9-for-53 with two extra-base hits since returning from a wrist injury and making his Red Sox debut on Aug. 11. His additional year of control could shift the narrative in 2027, but right now, it's Miller who has been the game-changing pickup.

Luis García Jr. Is the Yankees' Most Important Deadline Pickup in Decades

"Like the player, hate the fit, love the acquisition cost. So it's a mixed bag here."

That was my take on the Luis García Jr. trade at the time, and questions about how his first base/second base defensive profile would fit on a roster without glaring holes at those positions were reasonable.

However, the team needed offensive help, and he was hitting .283/.313/.560 for a 136 OPS+ with 23 home runs and 76 RBI at the time and came with an additional year of control.

Now that Giancarlo Stanton is likely done for the year and Aaron Judge has still not returned, the García trade has gone from a questionable fit to an absolute necessity for the Yankees offense.

The 26-year-old is batting .298/.343/.511 for a 135 OPS+ with five doubles, five home runs and 12 RBI in 102 plate appearances with the Yankees, and he is hitting primarily in the No. 3 and No. 4 spots in the lineup.

The question is no longer how he fits, but where the Yankees would be without him. The last time a deadline pickup had such a profound impact might be all the way back to David Justice in 2000.

articles.title: Predicting the AL East Finish and 2026 MLB Playoff Matchups For Yankees, Red Sox and More
articles.summary: The American League East is probably going to send three teams to the playoffs. The only questions are which ones, and in what arrangement?
articles.body:
The American League East is probably going to send three teams to the playoffs. The only questions are which ones, and in what arrangement?

We might as well take a whack at predicting how it all turns out, and then play the long game in projecting the playoffs for good measure.

This is partially about digging deep into what has happened in the AL East this season, and surmising what it could mean for potential rivalry renewals in October. It's also about the other teams each AL East contender could encounter in the postseason.

Read on for analysis that is bookended by predictions for how the AL East and the American League playoffs will play out.

Tampa Bay Rays: They actually did a bit of skidding in August, but have since won seven out of their last 10.

New York Yankees: As they await Aaron Judge's return, winning three out of four against the Red Sox this past weekend is part of an overall run in which they have won 12 out of 17.

Baltimore Orioles: A sweep at the hands of the Yankees in August slowed their roll, but they have since won eight out of their last 12.

Boston Red Sox: They're not cold , necessarily, but that incredible 32-5 run they went on has since been followed by an 11-14 slowdown since August 8.

Toronto Blue Jays: They're 20-12 since falling to a season-low 10 games under .500 back on July 28, but are more recently 6-5 in their last 11 even despite a sweep of the utterly hapless Seattle Mariners.

*Division winner, AL No. 1 seed ^No. 1 wild card ^^No. 2 wild card

The Rays do have one disadvantage for the remainder of the year, in that their schedule is the hardest of any team in the division.

Even so, the Rays only seem to immediately start ripping off Ws whenever it crosses my mind to doubt them. They're also 32-23 against teams with winning records, so their remaining schedule might be a mere inconvenience.

Why the Yankees and Red Sox Will Be Wild Cards

Both clubs are in a relatively safe position heading into the home stretch. The Yankees lead the Red Sox by 5.0 games for the top AL wild-card spot, while the latter has a 4.5-game edge on the Cleveland Guardians for the second.

Boston was positioned to make a move on New York heading into last weekend. Alas, losses in three out of four nixed that and gave the season series to the Yankees, to boot. The Red Sox also have the harder remaining schedule of the two.

Also, Aaron Judge could be back with the Yankees as soon as next week . With all respect to Roman Anthony and Trevor Story for what they bring to Boston, neither is a three-time MVP with creds as an all-time great hitter.

If the Rays grab the No. 1 seed and the Yankees and Red Sox grab the top two wild cards, the playoffs will be set up for an AL East collision course.

The Yankees and Red Sox would play a best-of-three in the Wild Card Series, with the winner moving on to face the Rays in the Division Series.

Matchup: Boston Red Sox vs. New York Yankees Format: Best of 3 Venue: Yankee Stadium Head-to-Head: Yankees 7, Red Sox 6

Though the Yankees outscored the Red Sox by 16 runs in their head-to-head matchups, that's largely fueled by a 16-1 blowout in their last meeting on Sunday. The truth is that the two teams were pretty evenly matched this year.

For the Yankees, the hope in a rematch would involve MLB's best starting pitching (i.e., 3.35 ERA) doing the carrying while Aaron Judge's return catalyzes an offense that has a typical calling card. Home runs tend to win games in October, and the Yankees lead the AL in long balls even with Judge hitting only 17 earlier in the year.

Just in the second half, though, Boston leads the AL in runs scored and home runs. That offense is even better with a healthy Roman Anthony, and it's not like this team can't pitch. The Red Sox's overall ERA is 3.66, fourth-best in baseball.

The X-factor is Willson Contreras, and specifically his strained left hamstring .

The Red Sox need him healthy and swinging a hot bat again. To this end, a .900 OPS and 26 home runs clearly mark him as Boston's best hitter. Yet his hamstring trouble did coincide with a cooldown, as he only had a .715 OPS in his last 23 games before landing on the IL.

5 Things That Could Derail NYY Title Run 😱

Matchup: Boston Red Sox/New York Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays Format: Best of 5 (2-2-1) Main Venue: Tropicana Field

The Rays being better than the sum of their parts usually is their whole thing, and you can see it this year in how their run differential (+51) pales in comparison to that of the Yankees (+115). They also don't have as many power threats, as they mostly rely on Junior Caminero to hit balls over the fence.

What the Rays can do that the Yankees aren't so good at is play good, clean baseball. Their pitchers have walked the fewest batters in baseball. They have the AL's most efficient defense. They steal bases and make productive outs to move runners over. And so on.

Home-field advantage could also be a deciding factor for the Rays. They are 47-25 at Tropicana Field, easily the best home winning percentage in the AL. The Yankees are good on the road, but not that good to the tune of a 43-29 record.

Three games in St. Petersburg between September 18 and 20 will decide this season's series. For now, Boston can take heart in having outscored the Rays by eight runs in their head-to-head meetings.

More so than the Yankees, the Red Sox can hang with the Rays in a clean baseball competition. The Red Sox also don't walk many batters, and they're just a tier below the Rays in Defensive Runs Saved . They're also not all about power offensively, as Boston has actually made more productive outs than the Rays have.

What could potentially further swing things in Boston's favor is their wealth of left-handed pitching. Against righties, Rays hitters are fifth in OPS. Against lefties, they're 21st in OPS.

Projected AL Wild Card Series: Cleveland Guardians vs. Houston Astros Projected AL No. 2 Seed: Chicago White Sox

On paper, not that solid. Yet it feels like it is.

The White Sox lead the Guardians by 3.0 games in the AL Central, and they have the easier remaining schedule of the two. The Astros are only 2.0 games ahead of the Texas Rangers in the AL West, yet are the lone contender in the division with a winning record since the All-Star break.

Hotness can also be what separates Cleveland in the wild-card race. The Guardians have four teams within 3.5 games of them, yet have been pulling away with wins in nine of their last 12.

Chicago White Sox: Their pitching is very shaky, but they're very good at hitting the long ball to the tune of 181 home runs, which ranks third among AL clubs.

Cleveland Guardians: Their 4.04 runs scored per game is the lowest of any projected playoff team, but nobody wants to face a starting trio of Gavin Williams, Parker Messick and Tanner Bibee.

Houston Astros: They have Yordan Alvarez leading an offense that's second in the AL with 184 home runs, and Hunter Brown is back to looking like a true Game 1 starter with a 2.63 ERA in his last seven starts.

The Yankees got the better of the Red Sox last weekend, but they also missed Boston's two best starting pitchers in Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle. That's a potential equalizer, and the Red Sox are ultimately more trustworthy when it comes to relief pitching and scoring runs in non-homer ways.

The Guardians are a sneaky-good road team at 37-32, so this is a question of whether Cleveland's arms or Houston's bats would win the day. The thinking here is that it's kind of a lopsided argument. As good as the Astros offense is, Yordan Alvarez is the only guy you really need to worry about.

If they knock off the Yankees, the Red Sox would be the best road team (40-31) left standing in the AL playoffs. Beyond that, they're more powerful than the Rays right now even though the Rays have one more home run for the season. Again, Boston leads the AL in runs and home runs since the All-Star break.

Cleveland Guardians vs. Chicago White Sox

As much as home runs tend to light the way in October, no team is more likely to break the rule than these White Sox. It can't be stressed enough just how shaky their starting pitching has become after posting a 6.21 ERA in August, and there's just not much there in terms of hope for October.

Here's where the Red Sox would finally have home-field advantage, and that could test even Cleveland's capacity for winning on the road. Boston has won 23 of its last 32 at Fenway Park.

The Guardians couldn't hope to win a slugfest, so they would need to pitch Boston into submission. Yet even that would be a tightrope, as the Red Sox's best pitchers are more than equal to the task of hanging with Cleveland's best pitchers.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani 'Not Close to Optimal' Amid Injury Woes, Struggles, Dodgers' Dave Roberts Says
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani's availability is in question after he struck out four times while batting Thursday night against the St. Louis Cardinals, according to Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
articles.body:
Shohei Ohtani's availability is in question after he struck out four times while batting Thursday night against the St. Louis Cardinals, according to Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.

Ohtani, who hasn't pitched since July 3 due to left knee issues , paused to shake out his arm while going 0-for-4 at the plate as the Dodgers conceded an 8-6 extra-innings loss.

Roberts said Wednesday night he felt an IL stint for Ohtani was a possibility but "very unlikely."

"If he's feeling the way that visibly looks, then really not helping anyone, so that's the conversation that I'll have with him," Roberts told reporters .

Roberts continued, "Clearly, tonight, you could see the swing wasn't the swing that we're used to seeing. So he's not close to optimal tonight."

Roberts said he planned to speak with both Ohtani and Dodgers head athletic trainer Thomas Albert before making any decisions about Ohtani's availability.

The Dodgers manager also expressed doubt, however, that a short break would help Ohtani get back to "100 percent" in time for the postseason.

"Is a day or two, or shoot, even 10 days, is that going to help get him to be 100 percent? Don't know the answer," Roberts said. "Where we're at, I think he's just going to have to find a way to make do, and do the best he can."

Ohtani had some big whiffs in a Wednesday night outing that marked the continuation of a down stretch for the Dodgers star, who has batted just .143 with four hits in 33 plate appearances over his last seven games.

He hasn't been the only player struggling for the Dodgers, which have gone 2-5 over that stretch.

Should Ohtani miss any time, the Dodgers will need its offense to do better than the 13 runners they stranded against the Cardinals in order to set themselves up for a World Series three-peat.

After going 13-16 since the start of August, the two-time defending MLB champions are in danger of losing out on a Wild Card round bye.

articles.title: Dave Roberts admits Shohei Ohtani is 'not close to optimal' after 4-strikeout performance
articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani didn't look like his usual self at the plate Wednesday.
articles.body:
Just hours after admitting Shohei Ohtani might not return to the mound this season , Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts offered some even more alarming quotes about the two-way star following Ohtani's four-strikeout performance in an 8-6 loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.

While a four-strikeout game as a hitter is never good, it was the way in which Ohtani racked up those whiffs that wound up being concerning. As some on X pointed out during a late-inning at-bat, Ohtani looked both stiff and late when trying to catch up to an elevated fastball.

After the contest — which the Dodgers lost in extra innings — Roberts said he was concerned about what he saw as well, per the Associated Press.

"I saw the same thing that everyone saw," Roberts said after an 8-6 loss in 10 innings to the St. Louis Cardinals. "You could see the swing wasn't the swing that we're used to seeing. He's not close to optimal."

Roberts said he would talk to Ohtani and the team's training staff about giving Ohtani a day off. Roberts added he didn't think a trip to the IL was necessary just yet.

Despite battling a knee injury — one that required an injection at the All-Star break — Ohtani hasn't missed many days in the second half, opting to push through it. But that might have to change after what Roberts saw during Wednesday's contest.

"I know he feels that he needs to post and be in the lineup and if he's upright he should play," Roberts said. "I respect that, but if he's feeling the way that he visibly looks, then it's really not helping anyone."

On the season, Ohtani's numbers at the plate are solid. The 32-year-old has a .279/.381/.525 slash line. His slugging is down compared to the past few seasons, but that's still an excellent line.

But in 41 games since the All-Star break, Ohtani is hitting .250/.333/.476. That would be a fine slash line for a normal player. For Ohtani, it represents a slump.

While the Dodgers can afford to lose Ohtani as a pitcher the rest of the way, missing out on his production as a hitter would have a far bigger impact. Given the team's record and star power, the Dodgers can afford to give Ohtani the time he needs to get right. A stint on the injured list doesn't appear to be on the table yet, but the Dodgers could consider it if Ohtani's struggles continue.

At this point in the season, the Dodgers' focus should be on making sure the team is at its best once the playoffs roll around. If that means Ohtani needs to rest more often, the team needs to make that a priority before the biggest games of the season are here.
